kurz: How robust different empirical findings are, how investment decisions can be derived from them and which three questions every investment idea has to pass.

bloecke.md:
At the end of this module on empirical evidence, there are many figures of varying robustness. Some findings follow from pure arithmetic and cannot be wrong. Others rest on data from several decades, many markets and asset classes. Still others are based on a single historical path that cannot be repeated. A considerable part of what appears as evidence in sales documents is a retrospective analysis of data that were searched specifically for this purpose.

To derive decisions from empirical findings, you have to keep these levels apart. Otherwise you treat an arithmetical rule like a hypothesis, or a hypothesis like an arithmetical rule.

bloecke.unter: The lower a statement is placed, the more it depends on the selection of the data and the greater the economic incentive to sell it.

bloecke.md:
## Statements that follow from arithmetic

In a three-page article in 1991, William Sharpe showed that the average actively managed unit of money must earn exactly the market return before costs, because active and passive investors together make up the market. After costs, it must necessarily earn less. The statement rests only on addition, subtraction, multiplication and division. It holds regardless of decade, country and asset class, and no new data series can refute it.

This does not rule out individual investors beating the market. But one investor's lead corresponds to another's shortfall, and fees weigh on both sides.

bloecke.titel: Who pays for the excess return
bloecke.md: Every claimed excess return must come at the expense of other investors. For an investment idea, it should be possible to name who structurally finances it and why this group is willing to lose permanently. If there is no answer, the idea is probably based on random patterns in past data.

## Broadly supported: the effect of costs

Costs are the only factor that works in the same direction in every major analysis, and the only one that is known in advance. For active equity UCITS in the EU, ESMA measures ongoing charges of 1.50% a year, compared with 0.53% for index funds and 0.31% for ETFs. Over the ten years to 2021, the active funds achieved a net return of 9.4%, against 10.6% for the index funds. The difference of around 1.2 percentage points is of the same order of magnitude as their cost difference of 0.97 points.

Morningstar approaches the question differently and reaches the same result. Over ten years, 27% of the funds in the cheapest fifth by cost beat comparable passive funds, but only 15% of those in the most expensive fifth. In the US large blend category, the figures were 15.4% against 3.9%. Of all the characteristics of a fund that can be observed in advance, only the expense ratio has stable predictive power.

bloecke.formel: Loss of wealth due to costs = 1 − ((1 + r − k) / (1 + r))^n
bloecke.erklaerung: Costs act as a factor that is applied again every year and do not simply add up. The loss is therefore smaller than k × n. At 1.3 percentage points over 30 years, it is around 31% instead of 39%. The result hardly depends on the level of the gross return; it is determined mainly by k and n.

bloecke.md:
## Broadly supported: the effect of diversification and holding period

Diversification narrows the range of outcomes; it does not promise a higher return. From 1988 to 2025, the DAX returned around 8.8% a year and the MSCI World in euros 8.5%. Restricting yourself to the home market therefore cost no return, but it brought greater fluctuations, with a standard deviation of 22.0% against 18.8%. Diversification above all reduces the risk that a single country or a single sector determines the result of your own portfolio.

Diversification, too, has visible limits. At the end of August 2026, US companies made up 72.1% of the MSCI World and information technology 29.8%, and the ten largest shares had a weight of 26.6%. “Globally diversified” therefore describes the distribution of the world's stock market value; the index does not reflect the distribution of its economic output.

A longer holding period works in the same direction but is less well supported than it seems. For the MSCI World (net, in euros), around 27% of all calendar years from 1970 to 2025 were negative, but none of the 42 rolling fifteen-year windows. For the S&P 500, there has been no negative twenty-year window since 1928. The worst, from 1929 to 1948, returned 2.4% a year.

bloecke.titel: Share of negative windows by holding period
bloecke.unter: MSCI World, net, in euros, 1970-2025, rolling calendar-year windows. The range narrows with a longer holding period; the analysis does not permit any further conclusions.

serien.name: Share of negative windows as a percentage

bloecke.md:
This window statistic is based on a single historical path. The 56 calendar years contain just under four non-overlapping fifteen-year periods, and the 42 windows count the same few periods several times over. If you derive a probability from this, you overestimate the amount of data by more than a factor of ten.

Adjusted for inflation, there were nevertheless long phases without growth. From 1966 to 1981 and again from 2000 to 2012, US equities returned around minus 0.8% a year after inflation in each case. The statement “always positive in the long run” applies to nominal calendar years in one sample and is not a promise.

## Broadly supported: the effect of your own behaviour

In the study “Mind the Gap”, Morningstar compares the return achieved by US funds with the return that reached the average invested dollar. In the decade to the end of 2025, these were 9.9% against 8.7% a year. The gap of 1.2 points arises solely from the timing and size of purchases and sales.

The gap is unevenly distributed. It is 0.4 points in the calmest fifth of funds, over 2.0 in the most volatile fifth and around 14 for crypto ETFs in 2024 and 2025. For broad US large blend funds it is exactly zero. The [[Investor return gap|investor return gap]] therefore arises from investors' behaviour and depends on how strongly a product tempts people to buy and sell. It disappears for products that are too boring to react to.

This finding is disputed as well. In the Financial Analysts Journal in 2026, Fulkerson, Jordan, Riley and Yan argue that poor timing costs considerably less than reported. The direction of the effect remains; its size is open.

## Unsupported statements

Below this level the data become thin, and this is where most sales material is found. The academic factor premiums for value, momentum, profitability and low risk exist. But they relate to cost-free long-short portfolios without trading costs and without limits on short selling. Only a fraction of this reaches a long-only product. Realistically, 0 to 2 percentage points over the market portfolio are more likely to remain after costs, and phases without excess return can last ten to twenty years. The size factor SMB returned minus 0.29% a year from January 1994 to July 2026. Over these thirty years, the premium was therefore absent.

bloecke.md:
## Three test questions

These findings yield a filter for investment ideas, but not a ready-made portfolio. It can be applied to any investment idea, from a certificate to a thematic fund to a tip from friends and acquaintances, and it works without a forecast.

schritte.text: Name the losers of the idea and the reason why they lose permanently, for example compulsion, regulation, deadlines, taxes or an information disadvantage. If the only answer is “the others are not paying attention”, check whether this group is large enough to finance your return and the fees. Publicly known ideas rarely have a large enough other side.

Check when the series shown begins and ends, and why exactly there. Establish whether funds that were closed are included and from which day the curve is real and not backfilled. Pay attention to gross or net, currency, transaction costs and taxes. Also ask who paid for the analysis.

Keep the position small enough that a decade of things going wrong remains bearable. In rolling twenty-year windows, the value factor was negative in 7.4% and the size factor in 19.5% of all cases. No investor's lifetime is long enough to be sure of collecting a premium. A mistake that can only be recognised after fifteen years may therefore only affect a small position.

bloecke.md:
A provider advertises a factor ETF with 3.0 percentage points of excess return a year since 2005, with ongoing charges of 0.35%.

As the other side (question 1), investors who systematically hold expensive growth shares come into consideration. That is plausible. But the premium has been published since the 1990s, and products with billions in assets exploit it deliberately.

On the data (question 2), it turns out that the ETF has only existed since 2019 and the years 2005 to 2018 are backfilled. This is exactly the boundary examined by the study “The Smart Beta Mirage”. According to it, the indices delivered an average excess return of around 3% a year before the launch of the respective ETF, and minus 0.5% to minus 1% after the launch.

After costs, 0 to 2 points are realistic (question 3). The factor can lose more than 50% in the interim, and phases without excess return can last up to twenty years. With a 10% share of the portfolio, the good case would leave 0.1 to 0.2 points for the portfolio as a whole.

The upshot is that the idea is not absurd. But its expected value is of the same order of magnitude as the additional costs and the uncertainty about the premium, and a verdict on it will be possible in fifteen years at the earliest.

- The ongoing product costs are stated in the key information document. They are the only figure in the sales material that is known in advance.
- Savings plans and rebalancing through new contributions instead of sales lower trading costs, because they avoid spreads and realised gains.
- Capital income is subject to 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) under Section 32d(1) EStG (Income Tax Act), plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge on it under Section 4 SolzG 1995 (Solidarity Surcharge Act). The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) is €1,000, or €2,000 for joint assessment (Section 20(9) EStG). If no exemption order (Freistellungsauftrag) is in place, it can be claimed via the capital income annex (Anlage KAP) of the tax return (Section 32d(4) EStG). Equity funds held as private assets benefit from a 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) under Section 20(1) sentence 1 InvStG (Investment Tax Act). Accumulating funds are taxed on an ongoing basis via the advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale) under Section 18 InvStG. Every sale brings the tax forward. The compound interest on the amount not yet paid is a measurable advantage of holding.
- The less eye-catching the product, the smaller the gap between fund return and investor return. It therefore depends less on the investor's character than on how the portfolio is structured.

In May 2026, Cremers, Fulkerson and Riley recalculated the SPIVA analysis. They weight by assets instead of by number of funds. For funds that were closed, they use the return achieved up to closure instead of counting these funds as losers across the board. They also compare with real index funds instead of with indices that nobody can buy. As a result, the share of US equity funds that lagged the benchmark over 20 years falls from 92% to 55%. For bond funds over ten years, the result is reversed. Instead of 71%, only 37% lag behind, so the majority are ahead of comparable passive funds.

The study was funded by the Active Managers Council of the Investment Adviser Association. That does not make it wrong, but it should be taken into account under the second test question. Two conclusions still hold after the correction. For equities, a majority of funds still lag behind, and no methodology makes it easier to pick the future winner. For bonds, on the other hand, the evidence for index-based investing is noticeably weaker than for equities. The usual presentation leaves out this difference.

Evidence looks backwards. It describes distributions that have occurred, but not your own portfolio over the next twenty years. Instead of a forecast, what makes sense is therefore a portfolio that still works if the coming two decades lie at the lower end of the historical range.

mitnehmen: Empirical statements carry different weight; arithmetic always holds, broad findings mostly hold, and window statistics from a single historical path hold only to a limited extent.
Costs are the only factor that is known in advance; 1.3 percentage points a year cost around 31% of final wealth over 30 years, not 39%.
Diversification and a long holding period narrow the range of outcomes, but they do not increase the expected return and are not a promise.
The investor return gap arises from investors' behaviour and is zero for products that hardly tempt people to trade.
Every investment idea can be tested with three questions: who on the other side pays for the excess return, which data are missing, and what a mistake costs until you notice it.

begriffe.text: Identity described by William Sharpe (1991). Since all investors together hold the market, the average active return before costs is exactly equal to the market return and, after costs, necessarily below it. The statement follows from an arithmetical rule and needs no empirical data.

Difference between the reported return of a fund and the return of the average invested unit of money. It arises solely from the timing and size of purchases and sales and grows with the volatility of the product.

Analysis of all overlapping sub-periods of equal length in a data series. It shows the range for each holding period but makes the amount of data seem larger than it is. From 56 years, 42 fifteen-year windows can be formed, but only just under four independent periods.

Part of a data series that was not used when developing a strategy, such as the period after a product's launch. Only in this part can an excess return count as a finding, because there it is not a consequence of the selection.
